papers_read.title_as_printed: Random forest model for feature-based Alzheimer's disease conversion prediction from early mild cognitive impairment subjects (Velazquez & Lee, PLoS ONE 16(4): e0244773, 2021)
Predicting conversion in cognitively normal and mild cognitive impairment individuals with machine learning: Is the CSF status still relevant? (Russo et al., Alzheimer's Dement. 2025;21:e14398)

what_each_reports.P-178: ADNI 1/2/GO early-MCI only: 383 patients (49 eventual AD converters, mean 5.02 years; 334 non-converters), 1806 visits with minority oversampling; 9 features (age, race, APOE4, hippocampal and ventricular volume, ADAS13, ADAS11, FAQ, MMSE); random forest. Test accuracy 0.936, AUC 0.96; majority-class baseline on the same test 0.900.
what_each_reports.P-308: ADNI cognitively normal plus MCI participants with baseline CSF, medication and neuropsychology data and 3-year follow-up: 648 participants, 90 converters within 3 years (CN to MCI, or MCI to AD). Non-converters undersampled, leaving 409 participants (22% converters). Gradient boosting with random-forest feature selection on standard clinical data, with no MRI. Whole cohort: training accuracy 91%, test accuracy 84% (specificity 96%, sensitivity 43%). CSF-positive sub-cohort test 88%, CSF-negative 86%. Logistic-regression models: AUC 0.85/0.87, accuracy 79%/78%.

quantity_a: Accuracy for eventual AD conversion (mean ~5 years) among early-MCI patients, visit-level oversampled, clinical scales plus hippocampal/ventricular MRI volumes
quantity_b: Accuracy for any one-step cognitive conversion within 3 years (CN to MCI, or MCI to AD) in a mixed CN+MCI cohort, subject-level, 22% converters after undersampling, standard clinical data and CSF without imaging
incompatible_if_same: No. Both accuracies are on imbalanced test sets with different majority rates, roughly 0.90 for P-178 and 0.78 for P-308, so each sits a similar distance above its own no-information rate. Neither gives an interval, and neither paper claims an ordering that the other refutes.

gates.task: mismatch: P-178 predicts EMCI-to-AD conversion; P-308 pools CN-to-MCI and MCI-to-AD conversion within 3 years (about 23% of its converters are CN-to-MCI)
gates.dataset_family: match: both ADNI; participants may overlap
gates.modality_family: mismatch: P-178 includes MRI volumes (hippocampus, ventricles) with clinical scales; P-308 uses no imaging (demographics, medications, neuropsychology, CSF t-tau/Abeta42)

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: accuracy in both, but endpoints differ (eventual AD in EMCI vs any 3-year one-step conversion in CN+MCI), as do class prevalence (~10-13% vs 22%) and sampling (oversampled visits vs undersampled subjects)
performance_validity: flag does not apply: 0.936 and 0.84 are below 0.97; P-308's 96% specificity is not an accuracy/AUC figure
independence: Distinct author groups; both ADNI, participants may overlap
grounds: P-178's outcome is eventual AD among early-MCI patients, whereas P-308's is any one-step conversion within 3 years in a mixed cognitively normal and MCI cohort, so the endpoint and population differ.
P-308 uses no MRI features and includes CSF, while P-178 includes MRI volumes and no CSF, so the predictor sets and modality families differ.
Both accuracies are on imbalanced test sets with different majority rates (0.900 vs about 0.78), so the raw 9.6-point gap does not compare like with like.
Neither paper reports uncertainty that would make the two figures mutually exclusive.

The participants were labeled as "converters" depending on whether their cognitive status progressed within 3 years, that is, (1) from CN to MCI; (2) from MCI to AD.

After undersampling, the model was applied to 409 participants (22% converters). With the optimal cut-off, the model's accuracy was 91% in the training set and 84% in the test set. The algorithm showed high specificity (96%) but low sensitivity (43%).
